{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "maintenance: update schedule before config

When running 'git maintenance start', the current pattern is to
configure global config settings to enable maintenance on the current
repository and set 'maintenance.auto' to false and _then_ to set up the
schedule with the system scheduler.

This has a problematic error condition: if the scheduler fails to
initialize, the repository still will not use automatic maintenance due
to the 'maintenance.auto' setting.

Fix this gap by swapping the order of operations. If Git fails to
initialize maintenance, then the config changes should never happen.", "report": "builtin/gc: fix crash when running `git maintenance start`

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with b6c3f8e12c (builtin/maintenance: fix
leak in `get_schedule_cmd()`, 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

Fix the regression by again unconditionally allocating the value in the
`out` parameter, if provided. Add a test that unsets the environment
variable to catch future regressions in this area."}

The `get_schedule_cmd()` function allows us to override the schedule
command with a specific test command such that we can verify the
underlying logic in a platform-independent way. Its memory management is
somewhat wild though, because it basically gives up and assigns an
allocated string to the string constant output pointer. While this part
is marked with `UNLEAK()` to mask this, we also leak the local string
lists.

Rework the function such that it has a separate out parameter. If set,
we will assign it the final allocated command. Plug the other memory
leaks and create a common exit path.", "report": "builtin/gc: fix crash when running `git maintenance start`

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with b6c3f8e12c (builtin/maintenance: fix
leak in `get_schedule_cmd()`, 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

Fix the regression by again unconditionally allocating the value in the
`out` parameter, if provided. Add a test that unsets the environment
variable to catch future regressions in this area."}

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "incoming": "builtin/gc: fix crash when running `git maintenance start`

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with b6c3f8e12c (builtin/maintenance: fix
leak in `get_schedule_cmd()`, 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

Fix the regression by again unconditionally allocating the value in the
`out` parameter, if provided. Add a test that unsets the environment
variable to catch future regressions in this area.", "choices": {"A": "maintenance: use random minute in systemd scheduler

The get_random_minute() method was created to allow maintenance
schedules to be fixed to a random minute of the hour. This randomness is
only intended to spread out the load from a number of clients, but each
client should have an hour between each maintenance cycle.

The previous implementation generated two template files with names
of the form 'git-maintenance@.(timer|service)'. The '.timer' or
'.service' indicates that this is a template that is picked up when we
later specify '...@<schedule>.timer' or '...@<schedule>.service'. The
'<schedule>' string is then used to insert into the template both the
'OnCalendar' schedule setting and the '--schedule' parameter of the
'git maintenance run' command.

Modify the template with a custom schedule in the 'OnCalendar' setting.
This schedule has some interesting differences from cron-like patterns,
but is relatively easy to figure out from context. The one that might be
confusing is that '*-*-*' is a date-based pattern, but this must be
omitted when using 'Mon' to signal that we care about the day of the
week. Monday is used since that matches the day used for the 'weekly'
schedule used previously.

Now that the timer files are not templates, we might want to abandon the
'@' symbol in the file names. However, this would cause users with
existing schedules to get two competing schedules due to different
names. The work to remove the old schedule name is one thing that we can
avoid by keeping the '@' symbol in our unit names. Since we are locked
into this name, it makes sense that we keep the template model for the
.service files.", "B": "maintenance: update schedule before config

When running 'git maintenance start', the current pattern is to
configure global config settings to enable maintenance on the current
repository and set 'maintenance.auto' to false and _then_ to set up the
schedule with the system scheduler.

This has a problematic error condition: if the scheduler fails to
initialize, the repository still will not use automatic maintenance due
to the 'maintenance.auto' setting.

Fix this gap by swapping the order of operations. If Git fails to
initialize maintenance, then the config changes should never happen.", "C": "Independent or insufficient evidence: no unique earlier decision needs review."}}

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with [ref] ([referenced subject], 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

Fix the regression by again unconditionally allocating the value in the
`out` parameter, if provided. Add a test that unsets the environment
variable to catch future regressions in this area.", "choices": {"A": "maintenance: use random minute in systemd scheduler

schedules to be fixed to a random minute of the hour. This randomness is
only intended to spread out the load from a number of clients, but each
client should have an hour between each maintenance cycle.

The previous implementation generated two template files with names
of the form 'git-maintenance@.(timer|service)'. The '.timer' or
'.service' indicates that this is a template that is picked up when we
later specify '...@<schedule>.timer' or '...@<schedule>.service'. The
'<schedule>' string is then used to insert into the template both the
'OnCalendar' schedule setting and the '--schedule' parameter of the
'git maintenance run' command.

Modify the template with a custom schedule in the 'OnCalendar' setting.
This schedule has some interesting differences from cron-like patterns,
but is relatively easy to figure out from context. The one that might be
confusing is that '*-*-*' is a date-based pattern, but this must be
omitted when using 'Mon' to signal that we care about the day of the
week. Monday is used since that matches the day used for the 'weekly'
schedule used previously.

Now that the timer files are not templates, we might want to abandon the
'@' symbol in the file names. However, this would cause users with
existing schedules to get two competing schedules due to different
names. The work to remove the old schedule name is one thing that we can
avoid by keeping the '@' symbol in our unit names. Since we are locked
into this name, it makes sense that we keep the template model for the
.service files.", "B": "maintenance: update schedule before config

When running 'git maintenance start', the current pattern is to
configure global config settings to enable maintenance on the current
repository and set 'maintenance.auto' to false and _then_ to set up the
schedule with the system scheduler.

This has a problematic error condition: if the scheduler fails to
initialize, the repository still will not use automatic maintenance due
to the 'maintenance.auto' setting.

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with b6c3f8e12c (builtin/maintenance: fix
leak in `get_schedule_cmd()`, 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "incoming": "builtin/gc: fix crash when running `git maintenance start`

It was reported on the mailing list that running `git maintenance start`
immediately segfaults starting with b6c3f8e12c (builtin/maintenance: fix
leak in `get_schedule_cmd()`, 2024-09-26). And indeed, this segfault is
trivial to reproduce up to a point where one is scratching their head
why we didn't catch this regression in our test suite.

The root cause of this error is `get_schedule_cmd()`, which does not
populate the `out` parameter in all cases anymore starting with the
mentioned commit. Callers do assume it to always be populated though and
will e.g. call `strvec_split()` on the returned value, which will of
course segfault when the variable is uninitialized.

So why didn't we catch this trivial regression? The reason is that our
tests always set up the "GIT_TEST_MAINT_SCHEDULER" environment variable
via "t/test-lib.sh", which allows us to override the scheduler command
with a custom one so that we don't accidentally modify the developer's
system. But the faulty code where we don't set the `out` parameter will
only get hit in case that environment variable is _not_ set, which is
never the case when executing our tests.

Fix the regression by again unconditionally allocating the value in the
`out` parameter, if provided. Add a test that unsets the environment
variable to catch future regressions in this area.", "choices": {"A": "Independent or insufficient evidence: no unique earlier decision needs review.", "B": "maintenance: update schedule before config

When running 'git maintenance start', the current pattern is to
configure global config settings to enable maintenance on the current
repository and set 'maintenance.auto' to false and _then_ to set up the
schedule with the system scheduler.

This has a problematic error condition: if the scheduler fails to

ddebfb3f61a71ad824b4dd5ee217d732d1ab9c78.content:
{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "pack-revindex: ensure that on-disk reverse indexes are given precedence

When an on-disk reverse index exists, there is no need to generate one
in memory. In fact, doing so can be slow, and require large amounts of
the heap.

Let's make sure that we treat the on-disk reverse index with precedence
(i.e., that when it exists, we don't bother trying to generate an
equivalent one in memory) by teaching Git how to conditionally die()
when generating a reverse index in memory.

Then, add a test to ensure that when (a) an on-disk reverse index
exists, and (b) when setting GIT_TEST_REV_INDEX_DIE_IN_MEMORY, that we
do not die, implying that we read from the on-disk one.", "report": "pack-write: skip *.rev work when not writing *.rev

Fix a performance regression introduced in a587b5a786 (pack-write.c:
extract 'write_rev_file_order', 2021-03-30) and stop needlessly
allocating the "pack_order" array and sorting it with
"pack_order_cmp()", only to throw that work away when we discover that
we're not writing *.rev files after all.

This redundant work was not present in the original version of this
code added in 8ef50d9958 (pack-write.c: prepare to write 'pack-*.rev'
files, 2021-01-25). There we'd call write_rev_file() from
e.g. finish_tmp_packfile(), but we'd "return NULL" early in
write_rev_file() if not doing a "WRITE_REV" or "WRITE_REV_VERIFY"."}

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "pack-write.c: extract 'write_rev_file_order'

Existing callers provide the reverse index code with an array of 'struct
pack_idx_entry *'s, which is then sorted by pack order (comparing the
offsets of each object within the pack).

Prepare for the multi-pack index to write a .rev file by providing a way
to write the reverse index without an array of pack_idx_entry (which the
MIDX code does not have).

Instead, callers can invoke 'write_rev_index_positions()', which takes
an array of uint32_t's. The ith entry in this array specifies the ith
object's (in index order) position within the pack (in pack order).

equivalent one in memory) by teaching Git how to conditionally die()
when generating a reverse index in memory.

wrong size, an unrecognized version, or similar.

It also jumps to this label when the reverse index couldn't be opened in
the first place, which will cause an error with the unguarded close()
call in the label.

file descriptor to close before attempting to close it.", "report": "pack-write: skip *.rev work when not writing *.rev

"pack_order_cmp()", only to throw that work away when we discover that
we're not writing *.rev files after all.

This redundant work was not present in the original version of this
code added in 8ef50d9958 (pack-write.c: prepare to write 'pack-*.rev'
files, 2021-01-25). There we'd call write_rev_file() from

write_rev_file() if not doing a "WRITE_REV" or "WRITE_REV_VERIFY"."}

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "difftool: implement the functionality in the builtin

The reason: this new, experimental, builtin difftool was shipped as part
of Git for Windows v2.11.0, to allow for easier large-scale testing, but
of course as an opt-in feature.

The motivation for converting the difftool is that Perl scripts are not at
all native on Windows, and that `git difftool` therefore is pretty slow on
that platform, when there is no good reason for it to be slow.

The current version of the builtin difftool does not, however, make full
use of the internals but instead chooses to spawn a couple of Git
processes, still, to make for an easier conversion. There remains a lot
of room for improvement, left later.

In addition, Perl does not really have access to Git's internals. That
means that any script will always have to jump through unnecessary
hoops, and it will often need to perform unnecessary work (e.g. when
reading the entire config every time `git config` is called to query a
single config value).

The speedup is actually more noticable on Linux than on Windows: a quick
test shows that t7800-difftool.sh runs in (2.183s/0.052s/0.108s)
(real/user/sys) in a Linux VM, down from  (6.529s/3.112s/0.644s), while on
Windows, it is (36.064s/2.730s/7.194s), down from (47.637s/2.407s/6.863s).
The culprit is most likely the overhead incurred from *still* having to
shell out to mergetool-lib.sh and difftool--helper.sh.", "report": "difftool: allow running outside Git worktrees with --no-index

As far as this developer can tell, the conversion from a Perl script to
a built-in caused the regression in the difftool that it no longer runs
outside of a Git worktree (with `--no-index`, of course).

It is a bit embarrassing that it took over two years after retiring the
Perl version to discover this regression, but at least we now know, and
can do something, about it.

This fixes https://github.com/git-for-windows/git/issues/2123"}

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "commit-graph write: add progress output

Furthermore, since the gc.writeCommitGraph setting was added in
d5d5d7b641 ("gc: automatically write commit-graph files", 2018-06-27),
there was no indication at all from a "git gc" run that anything was
different. This why one of the progress bars being added here uses
start_progress() instead of start_delayed_progress(), so that it's
guaranteed to be seen. E.g. on my tiny 867 commit dotfiles.git
repository:

Since we write the commit graph from the "git gc" process itself (as
opposed to what we do with say the "git repack" phase), we'd end up
writing the output to .git/gc.log and reporting it to the user next
time as part of the "The last gc run reported the following[...]"
error, see 329e6e8794 ("gc: save log from daemonized gc --auto and
print it next time", 2015-09-19).

With --stdin-packs we don't show any estimation of how much is left to
do. This is because we might be processing more than one pack. We
could be less lazy here and show progress, either by detecting that
we're only processing one pack, or by first looping over the packs to
discover how many commits they have. I don't see the point in doing
that work. So instead we get (on 2015-04-03-1M-git.git):

Before this change the "commit-graph write" command didn't report any
progress. On my machine this command takes more than 10 seconds to
write the graph for linux.git, and around 1m30s on the
2015-04-03-1M-git.git[1] test repository (a test case for a large
monorepository).

Note that here we don't show "Finding commits for commit graph", this
is because under "git gc" we seed the search with the commit
references in the repository, and that set is too small to show any
progress, but would e.g. on a smaller repo such as git.git with
--stdin-commits:", "report": "gc: fix regression in 7b0f229222 impacting --quiet

Fix a regression in my recent 7b0f229222 ("commit-graph write: add
progress output", 2018-09-17).  The newly added progress output for
"commit-graph write" didn't check the --quiet option.

Do so, and add a test asserting that this works as expected. Since the

The commit-graph feature is tested in isolation by
t5318-commit-graph.sh and t6600-test-reach.sh, but there are many
more interesting scenarios involving commit walks. Many of these
scenarios are covered by the existing test suite, but we need to
maintain coverage when the optional commit-graph structure is not
present.

To allow running the full test suite with the commit-graph present,
add a new test environment variable, GIT_TEST_COMMIT_GRAPH. Similar
to GIT_TEST_SPLIT_INDEX, this variable makes every Git command try
to load the commit-graph when parsing commits, and writes the
commit-graph file after every 'git commit' command.

There are a few tests that rely on commits not existing in
pack-files to trigger important events, so manually set
GIT_TEST_COMMIT_GRAPH to false for the necessary commands.

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "commit-graph: close descriptors after mmap

We don't ever refer to the descriptor after mmap-ing it. And keeping it
open means we can run out of descriptors in degenerate cases (e.g.,
thousands of split chain files). Let's close it as soon as possible.", "report": "commit-graph: retain commit slab when closing NULL commit_graph

So it happens to work out. But it still seems questionable to me that we
would clear a global slab (which might still be in use) when closing the
commit graph. This clearing comes from 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when
closing the graph, also release the slab, 2021-09-08), and was fixing a
case where we really did need it to be closed (and in that case we
presumably call close_object_store() more directly).

3. Later, when trying to write out a new commit graph, we'll ask for
     their tree oid via get_commit_tree_oid(), which will see that the
     object is parsed but with a NULL maybe_tree field. We'd then
     usually pull it from the graph file, but because the slab was
     cleared, we don't realize that we can do so! We end up returning
     NULL and segfaulting.

So I suspect there may still be a bug waiting to happen there, as any
object loaded before the call to close_object_store() may be stranded
with a bogus maybe_tree entry (and thus looking at it after the call
might cause an error). But I'm not sure how to trigger it, nor what the
fix should look like (you probably would need to "unparse" any objects
pulled from the graph). And so this patch punts on that for now in favor
of fixing the recent regression in the most direct way, which should not
have any other fallouts.

The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
making it a true noop when passed in an object_store with a NULL
commit_graph (it's OK to just return early, since the rest of its code
is already a noop when passed NULL). That restores the pre-ac6d45d11f
behavior. And that's what this patch does, along with a test that
exercises it (we already have a test that uses submodules along with
fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

2. Because we're using --recurse-submodules, we'll try to fetch each
     of the possible submodules. That implies creating a separate
     "struct repository" in-process for each submodule, which will
     require a later call to repo_clear()."}

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "commit-graph: move slab-clearing to close_commit_graph()

When closing and freeing a commit-graph, the main entry point is
close_commit_graph(), which then uses close_commit_graph_one() to
recurse through the base_graph links and free each one.

Commit 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when closing the graph, also release
the slab, 2021-09-08) put the call to clear the slab into the recursive
function, but this is pointless: there's only a single global slab
variable. It works OK in practice because clearing the slab is
idempotent, but it makes the code harder to reason about and refactor.

Move it into the parent function so it's only called once (and there are
no other direct callers of the recursive close_commit_graph_one(), so we
are not hurting them).", "report": "commit-graph: retain commit slab when closing NULL commit_graph

So it happens to work out. But it still seems questionable to me that we
would clear a global slab (which might still be in use) when closing the
commit graph. This clearing comes from 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when
closing the graph, also release the slab, 2021-09-08), and was fixing a
case where we really did need it to be closed (and in that case we
presumably call close_object_store() more directly).

Which at first glance seems like a bug we could already trigger. In the
situation described here, there is no commit graph in the submodule
repository, so our commit graph is NULL (in fact, in our test script
there is no submodule repo at all, so we immediately return from
repo_init() and call repo_clear() only to free up memory). But what
would happen if there was one? Wouldn't we see a non-NULL commit_graph
entry, and then clear the global slab anyway?

The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
making it a true noop when passed in an object_store with a NULL
commit_graph (it's OK to just return early, since the rest of its code
is already a noop when passed NULL). That restores the pre-ac6d45d11f
behavior. And that's what this patch does, along with a test that
exercises it (we already have a test that uses submodules along with
fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

The answer is "no", but for very bizarre reasons. Remember that
repo_clear() calls raw_object_store_clear(), which then calls
close_object_store() and thus close_commit_graph(). But before it does
so, raw_object_store_clear() does something else: it frees the commit
graph and sets it to NULL! So by this code path we'll _never_ see a
non-NULL commit_graph struct, and thus never clear the slab.

I do think there's some fragility here that we might want to follow up
on. We have a global commit_graph_data_slab that contains graph
positions, and our global commit structs depend on the that slab
remaining valid. But close_commit_graph() is just about closing _one_
object store's graph. So it's dangerous to call that function and clear
the slab without also throwing away any "struct commit" we might have
parsed that depends on it."}

When closing and freeing a commit-graph, the main entry point is
close_commit_graph(), which then uses close_commit_graph_one() to
recurse through the base_graph links and free each one.

Commit 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when closing the graph, also release
the slab, 2021-09-08) put the call to clear the slab into the recursive
function, but this is pointless: there's only a single global slab
variable. It works OK in practice because clearing the slab is
idempotent, but it makes the code harder to reason about and refactor.

Move it into the parent function so it's only called once (and there are
no other direct callers of the recursive close_commit_graph_one(), so we
are not hurting them).", "report": "commit-graph: retain commit slab when closing NULL commit_graph

So it happens to work out. But it still seems questionable to me that we
would clear a global slab (which might still be in use) when closing the
commit graph. This clearing comes from [ref] (commit-graph: when
closing the graph, also release the slab, 2021-09-08), and was fixing a
case where we really did need it to be closed (and in that case we
presumably call close_object_store() more directly).

Which at first glance seems like a bug we could already trigger. In the
situation described here, there is no commit graph in the submodule
repository, so our commit graph is NULL (in fact, in our test script
there is no submodule repo at all, so we immediately return from
repo_init() and call repo_clear() only to free up memory). But what
would happen if there was one? Wouldn't we see a non-NULL commit_graph
entry, and then clear the global slab anyway?

The answer is "no", but for very bizarre reasons. Remember that
repo_clear() calls raw_object_store_clear(), which then calls
close_object_store() and thus close_commit_graph(). But before it does
so, raw_object_store_clear() does something else: it frees the commit
graph and sets it to NULL! So by this code path we'll _never_ see a
non-NULL commit_graph struct, and thus never clear the slab.

The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
making it a true noop when passed in an object_store with a NULL
commit_graph (it's OK to just return early, since the rest of its code
is already a noop when passed NULL). That restores the pre-[ref]
behavior. And that's what this patch does, along with a test that
exercises it (we already have a test that uses submodules along with
fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

I do think there's some fragility here that we might want to follow up
on. We have a global commit_graph_data_slab that contains graph
positions, and our global commit structs depend on the that slab
remaining valid. But close_commit_graph() is just about closing _one_
object store's graph. So it's dangerous to call that function and clear
the slab without also throwing away any "struct commit" we might have
parsed that depends on it."}

This fixes a regression introduced in [ref] ([referenced subject], 2023-10-03), in which running:

Which at first glance seems like a bug we could already trigger. In the
situation described here, there is no commit graph in the submodule
repository, so our commit graph is NULL (in fact, in our test script
there is no submodule repo at all, so we immediately return from
repo_init() and call repo_clear() only to free up memory). But what
would happen if there was one? Wouldn't we see a non-NULL commit_graph
entry, and then clear the global slab anyway?

repo_clear() calls raw_object_store_clear(), which then calls
close_object_store() and thus close_commit_graph(). But before it does
so, raw_object_store_clear() does something else: it frees the commit
graph and sets it to NULL! So by this code path we'll _never_ see a
non-NULL commit_graph struct, and thus never clear the slab.

recurse through the base_graph links and free each one.

the slab, 2021-09-08) put the call to clear the slab into the recursive
function, but this is pointless: there's only a single global slab
variable. It works OK in practice because clearing the slab is

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "earlier": "commit-graph: avoid memory leaks

A fuzzer running on the entry point provided by fuzz-commit-graph.c
revealed a memory leak when parse_commit_graph() creates a struct
bloom_filter_settings and then returns early due to error. Fix that
error by always freeing that struct first (if it exists) before
returning early due to error.

While making that change, I also noticed another possible memory leak -
when the BLOOMDATA chunk is provided but not BLOOMINDEXES. Also fix that
error.", "report": "commit-graph: retain commit slab when closing NULL commit_graph

The bug is in step (2) above. We should not be clearing the slab when
cleaning up the submodule repository structs. Prior to ac6d45d11f, we
did not do so because it was done inside a helper function that returned
early when it saw NULL. So the behavior change from that commit is that
we'll now _always_ clear the slab via repo_clear(), even if the
repository being closed did not have a commit graph (and thus would have
a NULL commit_graph struct).

So I suspect there may still be a bug waiting to happen there, as any
object loaded before the call to close_object_store() may be stranded
with a bogus maybe_tree entry (and thus looking at it after the call
might cause an error). But I'm not sure how to trigger it, nor what the
fix should look like (you probably would need to "unparse" any objects
pulled from the graph). And so this patch punts on that for now in favor
of fixing the recent regression in the most direct way, which should not
have any other fallouts.

entry, and then clear the global slab anyway?

fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

The bug is in step (2) above. We should not be clearing the slab when

Which at first glance seems like a bug we could already trigger. In the
situation described here, there is no commit graph in the submodule
repository, so our commit graph is NULL (in fact, in our test script
there is no submodule repo at all, so we immediately return from
repo_init() and call repo_clear() only to free up memory). But what
would happen if there was one? Wouldn't we see a non-NULL commit_graph
entry, and then clear the global slab anyway?

The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
making it a true noop when passed in an object_store with a NULL
commit_graph (it's OK to just return early, since the rest of its code
is already a noop when passed NULL). That restores the pre-[ref]
behavior. And that's what this patch does, along with a test that
exercises it (we already have a test that uses submodules along with
fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

The answer is "no", but for very bizarre reasons. Remember that
repo_clear() calls raw_object_store_clear(), which then calls
close_object_store() and thus close_commit_graph(). But before it does
so, raw_object_store_clear() does something else: it frees the commit
graph and sets it to NULL! So by this code path we'll _never_ see a
non-NULL commit_graph struct, and thus never clear the slab."}

cleaning up the submodule repository structs. Prior to [ref], we
did not do so because it was done inside a helper function that returned
early when it saw NULL. So the behavior change from that commit is that
we'll now _always_ clear the slab via repo_clear(), even if the
repository being closed did not have a commit graph (and thus would have
a NULL commit_graph struct).

The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
making it a true noop when passed in an object_store with a NULL
commit_graph (it's OK to just return early, since the rest of its code
is already a noop when passed NULL). That restores the pre-[ref]
behavior. And that's what this patch does, along with a test that
exercises it (we already have a test that uses submodules along with
fetch.writeCommitGraph, but the bug only triggers when there is a
subsequent fetch and when that fetch uses --recurse-submodules).

So I suspect there may still be a bug waiting to happen there, as any
object loaded before the call to close_object_store() may be stranded
with a bogus maybe_tree entry (and thus looking at it after the call
might cause an error). But I'm not sure how to trigger it, nor what the
fix should look like (you probably would need to "unparse" any objects
pulled from the graph). And so this patch punts on that for now in favor

This fixes a regression introduced in ac6d45d11f (commit-graph: move
slab-clearing to close_commit_graph(), 2023-10-03), in which running:

3. Later, when trying to write out a new commit graph, we'll ask for
     their tree oid via get_commit_tree_oid(), which will see that the
     object is parsed but with a NULL maybe_tree field. We'd then
     usually pull it from the graph file, but because the slab was
     cleared, we don't realize that we can do so! We end up returning
     NULL and segfaulting.

So it happens to work out. But it still seems questionable to me that we
would clear a global slab (which might still be in use) when closing the
commit graph. This clearing comes from 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when
closing the graph, also release the slab, 2021-09-08), and was fixing a
case where we really did need it to be closed (and in that case we
presumably call close_object_store() more directly).

So I suspect there may still be a bug waiting to happen there, as any
object loaded before the call to close_object_store() may be stranded
with a bogus maybe_tree entry (and thus looking at it after the call
might cause an error). But I'm not sure how to trigger it, nor what the
fix should look like (you probably would need to "unparse" any objects
pulled from the graph). And so this patch punts on that for now in favor
of fixing the recent regression in the most direct way, which should not
have any other fallouts.", "choices": {"A": "commit-graph: close descriptors after mmap

monorepository)."}], "new": [{"id": "N1", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/6b89a34c89fc763292f06012318b852b74825619", "speaker": "Ævar Arnfjörð Bjarmason", "excerpt": "This test might be overly

{"goal": "Identify prior project decisions whose rationale should be revisited in light of new evidence.", "previous": [{"id": "P1", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/ac6d45d11f24921ead899c74569b717a7895f4a5", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "Commit 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when closing the graph, also release

idempotent, but it makes the code harder to reason about and refactor."}, {"id": "P4", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/ac6d45d11f24921ead899c74569b717a7895f4a5", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "When closing and freeing a commit-graph, the main entry point is

recurse through the base_graph links and free each one."}, {"id": "P5", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/c8828530b7797f5ab584c84dc2b86d3c14b39c8d", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "And keeping it
open means we can run out of descriptors in degenerate cases (e.g.,
thousands of split chain files)."}, {"id": "P6", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/ac6d45d11f24921ead899c74569b717a7895f4a5", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "commit-graph: move slab-clearing to close_commit_graph()"}, {"id": "P7", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/c8828530b7797f5ab584c84dc2b86d3c14b39c8d", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "Let's close it as soon as possible."}, {"id": "P8", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/c8828530b7797f5ab584c84dc2b86d3c14b39c8d", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "We don't ever refer to the descriptor after mmap-ing it."}], "new": [{"id": "N1", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/d70f554cdf38b0b05cfaa8e8eb9f80d54a5ae11c", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "So I suspect there may still be a bug waiting to happen there, as any

might cause an error)."}, {"id": "N2", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/d70f554cdf38b0b05cfaa8e8eb9f80d54a5ae11c", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "This clearing comes from 957ba814bf (commit-graph: when
closing the graph, also release the slab, 2021-09-08), and was fixing a
case where we really did need it to be closed (and in that case we
presumably call close_object_store() more directly)."}, {"id": "N3", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/d70f554cdf38b0b05cfaa8e8eb9f80d54a5ae11c", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "In the
situation described here, there is no commit graph in the submodule
repository, so our commit graph is NULL (in fact, in our test script
there is no submodule repo at all, so we immediately return from
repo_init() and call repo_clear() only to free up memory)."}, {"id": "N4", "source": "https://github.com/git/git/commit/d70f554cdf38b0b05cfaa8e8eb9f80d54a5ae11c", "speaker": "Jeff King", "excerpt": "The most immediate fix is to add in a NULL check in close_commit_graph(),
